title: Exponents, roots and absolute value
lines: Exponent questions look heavy but almost always collapse once you rewrite everything with the same base. Absolute value questions turn on one idea: distance is never negative, so one equation usually has two solutions.
## Exponent rules
- aᵐ × aⁿ = aᵐ⁺ⁿ and aᵐ ÷ aⁿ = aᵐ⁻ⁿ (same base only).
- (aᵐ)ⁿ = aᵐⁿ; (ab)ⁿ = aⁿbⁿ; (a/b)ⁿ = aⁿ/bⁿ.
- a⁰ = 1 for any a ≠ 0; a¹ = a.
- There is no rule for sums: aᵐ + aⁿ cannot be merged. Factor out the smaller power instead.
> Simplify (2³ × 2⁵) ÷ 2⁶ and (x²y³)².
> (x²y³)² = x⁴y⁶.
> Compute 2¹⁰ − 2⁸ and simplify 3²⁰ + 3²⁰ + 3²⁰.
> 3²⁰ + 3²⁰ + 3²⁰ = 3 × 3²⁰ = 3²¹.
! −2⁴ means −(2⁴) = −16, while (−2)⁴ = 16. A negative base raised to an even power is positive; to an odd power it stays negative.
## Equations with the same base
- If aˣ = aʸ with a not equal to 0, 1 or −1, then x = y. Rewrite both sides as powers of the same prime.
> Solve 4ˣ = 8ˣ⁻¹.
> 4 = 2² and 8 = 2³, so 2²ˣ = 2³ˣ⁻³.
> 2x = 3x − 3, so x = 3. Check: 4³ = 64 and 8² = 64.
! Bases 0, 1 and −1 break the rule: 1⁵ = 1⁹ although 5 ≠ 9. In QC, if a variable base could be 1 or −1, test it.
## Negative and fractional exponents
- a⁻ⁿ = 1/aⁿ, and (a/b)⁻ⁿ = (b/a)ⁿ. A negative exponent makes a reciprocal, not a negative number.
- a^(1/n) is the nth root of a; a^(m/n) = (nth root of a)ᵐ. Take the root first to keep numbers small.
> 27^(2/3): cube root of 27 is 3, and 3² = 9.
> 16^(−3/4): fourth root of 16 is 2, 2³ = 8, and the negative exponent gives 1/8.
## Roots
- √a × √b = √(ab) and √a ÷ √b = √(a/b) for a, b ≥ 0.
- Simplify by pulling out square factors: √50 = √(25 × 2) = 5√2. Only like roots add: 5√2 + 3√2 = 8√2.
- Rationalize: multiply top and bottom by the root. 6/√3 = 6√3/3 = 2√3.
- √x always means the nonnegative root. x² = 16 has two solutions, x = 4 or x = −4, but √16 = 4 only.
- √(x²) = |x|, not x.
> Simplify √50 + √18.
> √50 = 5√2 and √18 = 3√2, so the sum is 8√2 (about 11.3).
> Estimate √70.
> 8² = 64 and 9² = 81, so √70 is between 8 and 9, a little below 8.4 (8.4² = 70.56).
! For 0 < x < 1 the order flips: x² < x < √x. With x = 1/4: x² = 1/16, √x = 1/2.
## Scientific notation
- A number in the form a × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ a < 10. Multiply the a parts and add the exponents; then adjust so a is again between 1 and 10.
- Moving the decimal one place left raises the exponent by 1.
! 0.00052 = 5.2 × 10⁻⁴, not 10⁻³. Count the moves: the decimal point moves four places to reach 5.2.
## Absolute value
- |x| is the distance of x from 0, so |x| ≥ 0 always. |a − b| is the distance between a and b.
- |x| = k with k > 0 gives x = k or x = −k. |x| = −3 has no solution.
- |x| < k means −k < x < k. |x| > k means x < −k or x > k.
- |ab| = |a||b|, but |a + b| ≤ |a| + |b|, with equality only when a and b do not have opposite signs.
> Solve |x − 3| = 5.
> x − 3 = 5 gives x = 8; x − 3 = −5 gives x = −2. Both work.
> Solve |2x + 1| < 7.
! "The sum of all solutions" questions rely on you finding the negative case. For |x − 3| = 5 the sum is 8 + (−2) = 6.
## Comparing powers
- Make the bases or the exponents match. 2³⁰ = (2³)¹⁰ = 8¹⁰ and 3²⁰ = (3²)¹⁰ = 9¹⁰, so 3²⁰ is larger.
- For roots, raise both to a power that clears the fractions.
- Raising to a power keeps the order only when both numbers are positive.
> Which is larger, √5 or 3^(2/3)?
> Raise both to the 6th power: (√5)⁶ = 5³ = 125 and (3^(2/3))⁶ = 3⁴ = 81.
> Both are positive and 125 > 81, so √5 is larger (about 2.24 against 2.08).
## QC traps and shortcuts
- When a variable is raised to a power, test 0, 1, −1, a fraction like 1/2, and a negative fraction. Each class behaves differently: x³ > x² holds for x = 2 but fails for x = 1/2 and x = −2.
- Estimate huge numbers by their powers of 10 instead of multiplying.
- The on-screen calculator cannot show numbers like 3²¹ exactly; rules work faster than the calculator here.
> x < 0. Quantity A: x⁴. Quantity B: x³.
> x⁴ is positive for any nonzero x, and x³ is negative when x < 0. So Quantity A is greater for every allowed x.
